title: Functional mushrooms — benefits ranked by strength of evidence
purpose: Curated evidence database for the Balance AI agent to answer user questions about functional mushrooms. Benefits within each mushroom are ordered by strength of human evidence (rank 1 = best-supported).
sources_policy: Substance is drawn from PubMed / PubMed Central (peer-reviewed primary studies and systematic reviews) and Cochrane systematic reviews. Examine.com is included as a link-out reference only; its text is not reproduced.

evidence_scale.Limited: A systematic review / Cochrane review or several RCTs exist, but the evidence is low-quality or inconsistent. The most-studied claims sit here — 'studied', not 'proven'.
evidence_scale.Preliminary: A few small, short human trials show early signals; not yet robust.
evidence_scale.Preclinical/Traditional: Supported only by lab/animal studies or traditional use — no adequate human trials.
evidence_scale.Insufficient/Unproven: Studied in humans but no clear benefit demonstrated, or evidence too weak to judge.

agent_guidance: When answering users: (1) always state the evidence tier and that trials are typically small/short; (2) never present these as treatments or medical advice; (3) for anything involving a disease, medication, pregnancy, or cancer, tell the user to consult a doctor/pharmacist; (4) cite the linked sources; (5) do not invent benefits or doses beyond this database.
disclaimer: Educational information, not medical advice. Functional-mushroom evidence is generally early-stage. Consult a healthcare professional before use, especially with medications or a health condition.

mushrooms.name: Cordyceps
mushrooms.note: Species and extraction methods vary widely between studies, which limits comparability.

benefits.benefit: Aerobic exercise performance (VO2max, time to exhaustion, ventilatory threshold)
benefits.summary: Small RCTs and a meta-analysis report modest improvements in aerobic capacity in healthy/active adults and older adults. Effects are small and trials are short, heterogeneous, and sometimes industry-funded.
benefits.human_evidence: Meta-analysis of ~8 RCTs: modest VO2max gains; a 3-week RCT of C. militaris reported +4.8 mL/kg/min VO2max and +69.8 s time-to-exhaustion; a Cs-4 RCT improved aerobic capacity in healthy elderly.
benefits.caveats: Small samples, short durations, mixed species/doses; single-dose/acute effects less consistent.

sources.title: Cordyceps militaris ergogenic effects — narrative review (Nutrients, 2024)
Cs-4 aerobic capacity RCT in healthy elderly (Chin J Integr Med)

benefits.benefit: Chronic kidney disease — adjuvant to conventional care
benefits.summary: As an add-on to standard therapy, Cordyceps preparations may lower serum creatinine, raise creatinine clearance, and reduce proteinuria — but the Cochrane review rated the evidence low-quality, so no firm conclusions.
benefits.human_evidence: Cochrane review (Zhang 2014) and a later meta-analysis of Cordyceps as adjuvant in renal dysfunction.
benefits.caveats: Low-quality trials, mostly from settings using traditional Chinese medicine; adjuvant only, not a replacement for treatment.

sources.title: Cordyceps sinensis for chronic kidney disease (Cochrane, 2014)
Cordyceps as adjunct in renal dysfunction — systematic review & meta-analysis

benefits.summary: A systematic review/meta-analysis suggests oral Cordyceps as an add-on may improve lung-function and quality-of-life measures in stable COPD, but trial quality is limited.
benefits.human_evidence: Systematic review & meta-analysis of oral Cordyceps sinensis in stable COPD.
benefits.caveats: Heterogeneous, mostly lower-quality trials; adjunct only.

benefits.summary: Widely used traditionally for energy and immunity, with supportive lab/animal data, but adequate human RCTs are lacking.
benefits.human_evidence: Mechanistic and traditional-use evidence; no robust human trials for these specific claims.

benefits.summary: Cochrane reviews found benefits and harms unclear — not enough good evidence to judge.
benefits.human_evidence: Cochrane reviews on Cordyceps for kidney-transplant recipients and for hypertension.
benefits.caveats: Transplant/BP patients must not self-treat — interactions with immunosuppressants and BP meds.

mushrooms.name: Lion's Mane
mushrooms.note: Active compounds: hericenones (fruiting body) and erinacines (mycelium), which stimulate nerve growth factor (NGF). No dedicated Cochrane review exists yet.

benefits.benefit: Cognition with chronic use, incl. mild cognitive impairment
benefits.summary: Small RCTs report improved attention/working memory over weeks, and a 16-week trial improved cognition in older adults with mild cognitive impairment — but benefits faded after stopping.
benefits.human_evidence: 8-week RCT (n≈109) improved attention/memory; 16-week RCT in mild cognitive impairment; supported by a systematic review.
benefits.caveats: Small, short trials; benefits not durable after discontinuation.

sources.title: Benefits/side effects of H. erinaceus — systematic review

benefits.summary: Small studies report reduced stress and better mood/sleep with chronic use; early and not robust.
benefits.human_evidence: RCTs in healthy adults reporting mood/sleep improvements.
benefits.caveats: Small samples; not a treatment for mood disorders.

sources.title: Acute & chronic effects on cognition, stress and mood — RCT

benefits.summary: Lab/animal data show NGF stimulation and nerve-repair potential; human clinical evidence for nerve regeneration is not established.
benefits.human_evidence: Mechanistic reviews; no adequate human trials for nerve regeneration specifically.

sources.title: Neuroprotective properties of H. erinaceus — narrative review

benefits.summary: Acute single doses did not reliably improve overall cognition; only isolated task speed improvements seen.
benefits.human_evidence: Double-blind RCT of acute dosing in younger adults — mixed/null on global cognition.

mushrooms.name: Reishi
mushrooms.note: The only one of these three with a dedicated Cochrane review. Active constituents: polysaccharides (beta-glucans) and triterpenes.

benefits.benefit: Cancer care — adjuvant alongside chemotherapy/radiotherapy (NOT a standalone treatment)
benefits.summary: A Cochrane review of 5 RCTs (373 patients) found Reishi may increase tumour response when combined with conventional cancer treatment and could improve quality of life/immune markers, but the evidence was low to very-low quality. It should not be used as a sole cancer therapy.
benefits.human_evidence: Cochrane systematic review (Jin 2016): 5 RCTs, 373 participants; well tolerated, no major toxicity; low–very low quality evidence.
benefits.caveats: Adjuvant only; cancer patients must involve their oncologist. Never present as a cure.

benefits.summary: A GRADE-assessed systematic review/meta-analysis of clinical trials suggests possible effects on some CVD risk factors, but results are inconsistent and trials small.
benefits.human_evidence: GRADE-assessed systematic review & meta-analysis of clinical trials.
benefits.caveats: Inconsistent methods/formulations; not a substitute for cardiovascular treatment.

sources.title: Nutritional significance of G. lucidum — GRADE-assessed systematic review & meta-analysis

benefits.summary: Preclinical and some clinical data show immune-modulating effects (T/B lymphocytes, NK cells); human outcome evidence is early.
benefits.human_evidence: Clinical immune-marker changes reported alongside extensive preclinical data.

benefits.summary: Evidence does NOT support Reishi as a sole cancer treatment; the Cochrane review supports only adjuvant use.
benefits.caveats: Explicitly not supported — flag strongly to users.
